How these forecasts were built and tested

24 non-overlapping rolling-origin windows: the first 12 select the model and ensemble weights; the final 12 assess that frozen choice. Every fit uses only prices and matured training targets available at its origin. The unchanged-price forecast is retained unless validation MAE improves by at least 2%. Hyperparameters are fixed before testing. A current fit failure is explicitly labelled and falls back to no change.

ARIMA and damped exponential smoothing model log prices. AR(1)–GARCH with Student-t errors estimates the conditional return mean and volatility jointly: GARCH alone does not predict price direction. AI methods are Ridge, Extra Trees, gradient boosting and a small neural network; inputs are past returns, momentum and volatility, not an LLM or future news.

Each fit uses up to 630 past price observations or matured ML training examples. Fixed ML settings: Ridge penalty 50; 60 Extra Trees (depth 5); gradient boosting with 55 iterations; neural network with 24 and 12 hidden units. Feature and target scaling are fitted only on the training set. Unstable model forecasts implying more than a 100-fold forecast-horizon price change are rejected with a diagnostic, never clipped.

The central price is a back-transformed log-price estimate, not a guaranteed arithmetic mean. The displayed 90% range is calibrated from absolute rolling log-forecast errors; its coverage is approximate, not guaranteed. Illiquid unchanged quotes can make measured errors and ranges artificially small. Scheduled event dates are predictors; exact dividend/corporate-action price adjustments are not mechanically imposed. Unannounced earnings/news, spreads and execution prices remain outside these forecasts. NAV expenses are already embedded. Forecasts do not override the existing BUY / WAIT / HOLD / SELL rules.

Cross-asset models: the three dependency models add lagged S&P 500 USD returns, leave-one-out Baltic and fund return factors, and five peers selected by absolute correlation inside each trailing 252-observation training window. All external return series are delayed by two business days. Inputs include lagged returns, 5/7/20-observation averages, 7/20-observation volatility, 7-observation beta and trailing 7/60-observation correlations with the target. Correlation is a predictor, not a claim of causation. The same conservative lag is used in validation and live forecasts.

Dependency Ridge uses penalty 100; the tree models use the fixed settings above. Missing predictors are replaced by zero within the fitted pipeline; scaling and mature-target training use training data only. The current instrument universe is fixed, so survivorship bias remains possible. Historical fund NAV publication timestamps are unavailable; the two-day buffer is an assumption, not proof of historical execution availability. The original independent-model ensemble remains frozen; the added models compete individually using the first 12 windows. The final 12 windows evaluate the frozen choice.

Seven-observation inputs: compounded and average return, SD, downside/upside deviation, Sharpe, Sortino, Omega, Calmar-style return/drawdown, empirical VaR/CVaR, drawdown, ulcer index, skewness, kurtosis, positive/unchanged-return fractions and autocorrelation. Ratios use zero risk-free return and zero minimum acceptable return; they are not annualised. With seven observations, empirical 95% CVaR reduces to the worst observation, so it is a noisy short-window feature, not a reliable tail-risk estimate. Undefined performance ratios have an explicit indicator and a neutral model placeholder.

Calendar inputs: upcoming 1/7-business-day and recent 7-calendar-day counts by event type, plus weekday/month seasonality. Historical schedule dates are used only when the exact date is verified in a timestamped publication. Unverified schedules and the BLS macro calendar are available only from the current snapshot date; they are never backdated. The schedule is not exhaustive and uses event dates, not intraday release times; after-close announcements may affect the next trading session. An event date does not reveal an earnings surprise or guarantee a price direction. Event categories absent from training have no demonstrated learned effect. Predictors that were constant in every past usable feature row are held at their training value for the live neural forecast, preventing random neural responses to first-ever calendar inputs; this changes no historical validation/test input. Unannounced earnings/news, spreads and execution prices remain outside these forecasts. NAV expenses are already embedded. Forecasts do not override the existing BUY / WAIT / HOLD / SELL rules.

Cross-asset models: the three dependency models add lagged S&P 500 USD returns, leave-one-out Baltic and fund return factors, and five peers selected by absolute correlation inside each trailing 252-observation training window. All external return series are delayed by two business days. Inputs include lagged returns, 5/7/20-observation averages, 7/20-observation volatility, 7-observation beta and trailing 7/60-observation correlations with the target. Correlation is a predictor, not a claim of causation. The same conservative lag is used in validation and live forecasts.

Dependency Ridge uses penalty 100; the tree models use the fixed settings above. Missing predictors are replaced by zero within the fitted pipeline; scaling and mature-target training use training data only. The current instrument universe is fixed, so survivorship bias remains possible. Historical fund NAV publication timestamps are unavailable; the two-day buffer is an assumption, not proof of historical execution availability. The original independent-model ensemble remains frozen; the added models compete individually using the first 12 windows. The final 12 windows evaluate the frozen choice.

Seven-observation inputs: compounded and average return, SD, downside/upside deviation, Sharpe, Sortino, Omega, Calmar-style return/drawdown, empirical VaR/CVaR, drawdown, ulcer index, skewness, kurtosis, positive/unchanged-return fractions and autocorrelation. Ratios use zero risk-free return and zero minimum acceptable return; they are not annualised. With seven observations, empirical 95% CVaR reduces to the worst observation, so it is a noisy short-window feature, not a reliable tail-risk estimate. Undefined performance ratios have an explicit indicator and a neutral model placeholder.

Calendar inputs: upcoming 1/7-business-day and recent 7-calendar-day counts by event type, plus weekday/month seasonality. Historical schedule dates are used only when the exact date is verified in a timestamped publication. Unverified schedules and the BLS macro calendar are available only from the current snapshot date; they are never backdated. The schedule is not exhaustive and uses event dates, not intraday release times; after-close announcements may affect the next trading session. An event date does not reveal an earnings surprise or guarantee a price direction. Event categories absent from training have no demonstrated learned effect. Predictors that were constant in every past usable feature row are held at their training value for the live neural forecast, preventing random neural responses to first-ever calendar inputs; this changes no historical validation/test input. The volatility proxy is shrunk halfway toward the training RMS baseline and bounded by the range of its training targets to prevent numerical extrapolation. Models also forecast realised variation using matured targets; conditional-scale-normalised residuals calibrate prediction ranges, with held-out coverage assessed separately.

How these forecasts were built and tested

24 non-overlapping rolling-origin windows: the first 12 select the model and ensemble weights; the final 12 assess that frozen choice. Every fit uses only prices and matured training targets available at its origin. The unchanged-price forecast is retained unless validation MAE improves by at least 2%. Hyperparameters are fixed before testing. A current fit failure is explicitly labelled and falls back to no change.

ARIMA and damped exponential smoothing model log prices. AR(1)–GARCH with Student-t errors estimates the conditional return mean and volatility jointly: GARCH alone does not predict price direction. AI methods are Ridge, Extra Trees, gradient boosting and a small neural network; inputs are past returns, momentum and volatility, not an LLM or future news.

Each fit uses up to 630 past price observations or matured ML training examples. Fixed ML settings: Ridge penalty 50; 60 Extra Trees (depth 5); gradient boosting with 55 iterations; neural network with 24 and 12 hidden units. Feature and target scaling are fitted only on the training set. Unstable model forecasts implying more than a 100-fold forecast-horizon price change are rejected with a diagnostic, never clipped.

The central price is a back-transformed log-price estimate, not a guaranteed arithmetic mean. The displayed 90% range is calibrated from absolute rolling log-forecast errors; its coverage is approximate, not guaranteed. Illiquid unchanged quotes can make measured errors and ranges artificially small. Scheduled event dates are predictors; exact dividend/corporate-action price adjustments are not mechanically imposed. Unannounced earnings/news, spreads and execution prices remain outside these forecasts. NAV expenses are already embedded. Forecasts do not override the existing BUY / WAIT / HOLD / SELL rules.

Cross-asset models: the three dependency models add lagged S&P 500 USD returns, leave-one-out Baltic and fund return factors, and five peers selected by absolute correlation inside each trailing 252-observation training window. All external return series are delayed by two business days. Inputs include lagged returns, 5/7/20-observation averages, 7/20-observation volatility, 7-observation beta and trailing 7/60-observation correlations with the target. Correlation is a predictor, not a claim of causation. The same conservative lag is used in validation and live forecasts.

Dependency Ridge uses penalty 100; the tree models use the fixed settings above. Missing predictors are replaced by zero within the fitted pipeline; scaling and mature-target training use training data only. The current instrument universe is fixed, so survivorship bias remains possible. Historical fund NAV publication timestamps are unavailable; the two-day buffer is an assumption, not proof of historical execution availability. The original independent-model ensemble remains frozen; the added models compete individually using the first 12 windows. The final 12 windows evaluate the frozen choice.

Seven-observation inputs: compounded and average return, SD, downside/upside deviation, Sharpe, Sortino, Omega, Calmar-style return/drawdown, empirical VaR/CVaR, drawdown, ulcer index, skewness, kurtosis, positive/unchanged-return fractions and autocorrelation. Ratios use zero risk-free return and zero minimum acceptable return; they are not annualised. With seven observations, empirical 95% CVaR reduces to the worst observation, so it is a noisy short-window feature, not a reliable tail-risk estimate. Undefined performance ratios have an explicit indicator and a neutral model placeholder.

Calendar inputs: upcoming 1/7-business-day and recent 7-calendar-day counts by event type, plus weekday/month seasonality. Historical schedule dates are used only when the exact date is verified in a timestamped publication. Unverified schedules and the BLS macro calendar are available only from the current snapshot date; they are never backdated. The schedule is not exhaustive and uses event dates, not intraday release times; after-close announcements may affect the next trading session. An event date does not reveal an earnings surprise or guarantee a price direction. Event categories absent from training have no demonstrated learned effect. Predictors that were constant in every past usable feature row are held at their training value for the live neural forecast, preventing random neural responses to first-ever calendar inputs; this changes no historical validation/test input. The volatility proxy is shrunk halfway toward the training RMS baseline and bounded by the range of its training targets to prevent numerical extrapolation. 1.4. Active stochastic netSD portfolios — 1124 training observations

Active history rule: 70 eligible assets; 1124 training observations (2021-11-29–2026-05-08) and 126 separate diagnostic observations (2026-05-11–2026-11-04). Short-history instruments are excluded from decisions and the dominance reference set. All 12 current holdings remain available. Fund NAV already includes ongoing fees.

126-day segment is a descriptive fixed-allocation diagnostic, not an independent strategy backtest: current forecast centres use data through their current origin. Official data refreshed 2026-11-06T09:11:31.288796+02:00: share closes through 2026-11-05; latest available EUR fund NAV dates 2026-11-04. Each profile states its own observation date. Weekly models, joint scenarios, technical signals and allocations are refitted from this snapshot. The new canonical netSD reference network contains the 70 eligible assets and Current, with one training-derived denominator. Old comparison policies containing excluded holdings are not silently projected or backfilled. The S&P 500 benchmark uses USD price returns; currency and dividend bases differ from EUR assets, and benchmark measures use only matching US trading dates.

Maximum common history: 1250 aligned daily returns; the earliest 1124 form the training sample and the latest 126 form the diagnostic segment. No earlier common observations were discarded. Investor exclusions: AIR, EJTC, FRGTE, MAGIC, SE0029504588. Ineligible shorter histories are retained in the private archive.

Historical portfolio series apply constant origin-price weights to daily asset returns: they are hypothetical daily-rebalanced diagnostics, not realised account histories or buy-and-hold share-quantity backtests. The future scenario policy instead tracks integer holdings and cash through its two decision stages. — denotes a native R function that is undefined for the selected sample; no replacement ratio is invented.

Purchase signal restrictions removed (5 November 2026): both stages may purchase without technical BUY votes and without a positive conditional remaining forecast. Purchases are chosen by the scenario-expected netSD minus penalties objective. The EUR 750 initial additional purchase limit per asset, EUR 15,000 total budget, integer lots, zero to four funds, history and liquidity restrictions, and zero-interest cash remain. Technical indicators remain diagnostics. Recourse sales still require a negative conditional forecast and at least 3 SELL votes; the no-sales policy prohibits all sales. Recourse decisions remain common to scenarios sharing the same observed prefix; future scenario identity is never disclosed.

Confirmed actual holdings: last confirmed 2026-11-05T12:24:10.997072+02:00. Current quantities are actual holdings; unexecuted model purchases are shown separately as targets. Valuations use the report market snapshot. Actual execution prices were not supplied, so portfolio values are not presented as transaction costs or realised account profit.

Daily and weekly-frequency forecasts: five joint scenario clusters

Snapshot 2026-11-05; shared target 2026-12-03. Daily models forecast 20 dated points over 4 weeks. Weekly models fit non-overlapping genuine weekly observations and forecast exactly 4 weekly steps. Weekly boundaries follow the snapshot weekday; they are not necessarily Friday closes. Each bin uses only its last actual price/NAV dated on or before that boundary; empty weeks are never filled. Weekly-only features use 4/13/26-week windows. Nine model families and a validation ensemble are fitted separately from daily-frequency models, with 12 validation origins followed by 12 held-out weekly origins. Selection uses validation data only. Within each diagnostic block the four-week forecast windows overlap, so errors are dependent; three weekly origins are purged between validation and held-out blocks to prevent their target windows from crossing. The portfolio remains a two-stage policy with one recourse decision after two observed daily steps, not a four-stage weekly rebalancing strategy.

13 daily-method and 10 weekly-method joint-asset scenarios are pooled into five shared clusters. The daily family receives 50% total prior weight and the weekly family 50%, divided equally among the methods in each family. These are modelling priors, not calibrated probabilities or independent new information. Five clusters do not mean five observable information nodes: four two-day price-prefix nodes remain, with 5 clusters × 4 terminal regimes × 4 information nodes = 80 weighted leaves. Neither future cluster identity nor future regimes are observable at recourse.

Intraperiod assumption: a weekly model produces a price at each weekly boundary. Intermediate daily scenario prices use the mean daily log-price shape corrected separately between each pair of weekly forecast anchors, over open sessions only. These are endpoint-constrained modelled bridges, not direct weekly-model predictions. Joint weighted KMeans clusters use all 70 terminal log returns scaled by training-only volatility; cluster paths are geometric centroids. Missing individual methods fall back explicitly to unchanged price; no asset is silently removed.

Clustering retains 57.69% of the pooled cross-scenario terminal log-return variance. Reduction can smooth tail outcomes. Both unreduced scenarios and memberships remain in the private audit. Forecast diagnostics do not establish independent investment-strategy performance. Daily and weekly models share underlying observations, and historical NAV publication timestamps are incomplete.

The main plan prohibits initial sales. The separate both-stage comparison permits an initial sale only with a negative mean terminal forecast and at least three of four current SELL votes. Recourse sales use the corresponding node conditions.

\[\max_{q^0,\{q^n\}}\sum_s\pi_s\left[\frac{\mathrm{OUT}_s-\mathrm{IN}_s}{D}-\operatorname{Penalty}(q^{n(s)},p_{\tau,s})\right],\quad q_i^0,q_i^n\in\mathbb Z_+,\quad q^0\ge q^{current},\quad p_0^\top q^0\le15000,\quad 0\le(q_i^0-q_i^{current})_+\le b_i^0\lfloor750/p_{0i}\rfloor.\]

Every scenario compares the 1124 historical returns plus all forecast-period daily returns. The 126 diagnostic observations are excluded from historical netSD scoring and factor regression. D is recomputed from the training-only reference network. Zero to four whole-unit funds are allowed; no technical entry signal is required. A first-stage purchase does not require BUY votes and is capped at EUR 750 per asset; unused budget stays as zero-interest cash. Recourse purchases require neither BUY votes nor a positive conditional remaining forecast; their quantities are selected by the optimisation objective under the remaining constraints. Minimum new-share lots of ten, fund entry size of EUR 300, existing liquidity limits and the original penalty remain. The minimum historical mean compares both alternatives at the same node and total budget, including uninvested cash. A recourse sale additionally requires a negative conditional forecast and at least three of four native TTR SELL signals. The no-sales comparison imposes qⁿ ≥ q⁰.

\[q_i^n\le q_i^0+b_i^n\bar q_i,\quad b_i^n=1,\quad c_0=15000-p_0^\top q^0\ge0.\]
\[b_i^0=1,\quad q_i^n\ge(1-a_i^n)q_i^0,\quad 0\le q_i^n\le\bar q_i,\quad p_n^\top q^n+c_n=p_n^\top q^0+c_0,\quad c_n\ge0.\]

Mathematical model — no initial sales; gated recourse
$$ \max_{q_0,c_0,\{q_{n(s)},c_s\}_{s=1}^{S}}\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^{S}\left[\frac{OUT_s(\mathcal R_s)-IN_s(\mathcal R_s)}{D}-P_s(q_{n(s)})\right]. $$
$$ q_{i0}\ge q_i^{\mathrm{Current}},\quad c_0=B-\sum_i p_{i0}q_{i0}\ge0,\quad q_{i0},q_{in}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}. $$
$$ a_{is}=\mathbf1\{p_{iTs}
$$ c_s=c_0+\sum_i p_{i\tau s}(q_{i0}-q_{i,n(s)})\ge0,\quad p_{0:\tau,s}=p_{0:\tau,s'}\Longrightarrow q_{n(s)}=q_{n(s')}. $$
$$ V_{ts}=\begin{cases}p_{ts}^{\mathsf T}q_0+c_0,&t\le\tau,\\p_{ts}^{\mathsf T}q_{n(s)}+c_s,&t>\tau,\end{cases}\quad r_{ts}=\frac{V_{ts}}{V_{t-1,s}}-1,\quad \mathcal R_s=\{H_t^{\mathsf T}w_s^{\mathrm{backcast}}\}_{t=1}^{N}\cup\{r_{1s},\ldots,r_{Ts}\}. $$
$$ w_{is}^{\mathrm{backcast}}=\frac{p_{i\tau s}q_{i,n(s)}}{p_{\tau s}^{\mathsf T}q_{n(s)}+c_s},\quad 2\le\sum_{i\in\mathcal F}\mathbf1\{q_{i0}>0\}\le4,\quad 2\le\sum_{i\in\mathcal F}\mathbf1\{q_{in}>0\}\le4. $$
$$ 0\le q_{i0},q_{in}\le u_i,\quad q_{i0},q_{in}\in\{0,10,11,\ldots\}\quad(i\text{ a new share}),\\ q_{i0}=0\ \text{or}\ p_{i0}q_{i0}\ge300,\quad q_{in}=0\ \text{or}\ p_{i\tau s}q_{in}\ge300\quad(i\in\mathcal F,\ s:n(s)=n),\\ \frac{\sum_i\mu_i p_{i\tau s}q_{i,n(s)}}{\sum_i p_{i\tau s}q_{i,n(s)}}\ge\mu_{\mathrm{Current}}\quad(\forall s). $$
$$ P_s=0.00015\,n_{\mathrm{new},s}^{2}+\frac{0.001}{\sum_i\widetilde w_{is}^{2}} +0.006\sum_{i\in\mathcal N_s}\left(\frac{(0.01-\widetilde w_{is})_+}{0.01}\right)^2\\ +0.006\sum_{\substack{i\in\mathcal E\\q_{i,n(s)}>0}}\frac{(10-q_{i,n(s)}d_i)_+}{10} +0.002\sum_{\substack{i\in\mathcal E\\v_i>0}}\left(\frac{5q_{i,n(s)}}{v_i}\right)^2, \qquad\widetilde w_{is}=\frac{p_{i\tau s}q_{i,n(s)}}{\sum_jp_{j\tau s}q_{j,n(s)}}. $$

i indexes all eligible instruments; s indexes thirteen equiprobable joint forecast scenarios; n(s) is the information node identified only by the complete observed price prefix through τ = 2 (3 November); T = 5; B = EUR 15,000; D = 175. q is whole units, p is EUR price/NAV, c is nonnegative cash, H is the historical asset-return vector, and v with a SELL superscript is an individual indicator vote. If a = 0, sales are prohibited, including sales of units bought in stage one. If a = 1, a sale is permitted, not required. Identical observed prefixes share one decision; scenario labels and prices after τ do not determine the information node. The model uses forecast information for the remaining week at that node, never realised future observations.

𝓕 denotes funds, 𝓔 shares, 𝓝 newly introduced shares, d the historical five-year average annual cash dividend per unit, vᵢ the smaller of recent and median weekly traded volume, and uᵢ the audited unit cap. n_new counts newly introduced share positions; μ is the historical mean return. Shares with nonpositive historical individual netSD, excluded shares and shares failing the trading-activity rule cannot be increased: uᵢ = Current units. Otherwise uᵢ = max(Current units, floor(vᵢ/5)); NAV funds are volume-exempt. The penalty weights use invested-asset weights excluding cash, while historical-return backcast weights include cash in their denominator, matching the existing implementation. Each node order must satisfy cash feasibility, fund minima and gates in every scenario sharing that node. The same historical post-recourse backcast as the original model is retained explicitly; the historical block is not fixed at q₀. Fund expenses already enter NAV. Seven-thread neighbourhood search is heuristic; no global optimality certificate is claimed.

Scope: VSS, EVPI, EV, EEV, RP and WS in this audit refer to the original no-sale benchmark, not the corrected gated-recourse policy. The current main plan is in 1.4.a–e.

1.4.f. No-sale baseline: VSS, EVPI and scenario-dependence audit

All values use the same EUR 15,000 budget, current holdings, no-sales rule, whole units, liquidity caps, mean-return floor, two-to-four-fund requirement, reference universe, denominator 175 and existing penalty. The 13 scenarios have equal probability. The deterministic EV problem uses the arithmetic mean of the joint price paths; all comparison-asset forecast returns are rebuilt from that mean path. EV is not section 1.3.

$$ \widehat{\mathrm{VSS}}=\widehat z_{RP}-\widehat z_{EEV},\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{EVPI}}=\widehat z_{WS}-\widehat z_{RP}. $$

Objective-score units, not euros or expected-return percentages. The objective is netSD minus the portfolio penalty. EEV fixes only the EV first-stage units; its second-stage decisions obey the original information-node partition. WS lets the first-stage decision depend on the full future scenario, which is not possible in actual trading.

Solver limitation: these are heuristic estimates, not certified optimal VSS/EVPI. The same seven-thread integer neighbourhood search is used throughout. The existing saved policy scores 0.830230356; the diagnostic RP re-solve scores 0.834681751. The saved-policy gap against EEV is -0.003507444. A negative saved-policy gap reveals unfinished optimisation, not negative true VSS. The diagnostic re-solve is not substituted into the active trade tables.

The per-search iteration limit is 12. The following searches still improved at that limit: EEV, RP_refined, WS_02, WS_06, WS_08, WS_09, WS_12. The uncertainty from incomplete optimisation has not been quantified; differences must not be treated as precise economic values.

What drives these estimates: EEV, RP and WS all average netSD 0.868571429. Their penalised-objective differences therefore come from the portfolio penalty, not an increase in average netSD. This is a comparison of these particular heuristic policies; it is not the VSS of a separately optimised unpenalised model.

Diagnostics computed: 2026-11-02T07:42:22.741451+00:00. Market prices and the active allocation were not refreshed by this calculation.

How cross-asset dependence enters the scenarios

No mixing of forecasting methods between assets: scenario Gradient boosting uses the Gradient boosting path for every eligible asset; the same applies to each of the 13 method labels. Validation ensemble is an exception only in the sense that its asset-specific internal model weights can differ. Current inputs contain no missing-method fallback paths.

Historical dependence is retained: portfolio historical returns are calculated from aligned same-date asset returns. The model does not shuffle individual asset observations. An explicit covariance matrix is not a separate constraint or objective term in this netSD model.

Forecast dependence is partial: Dependency Ridge, Dependency Extra Trees and Dependency Gradient boosting include lagged market/fund factors, S&P 500, five training-selected peers, trailing correlations and beta. The selection uses up to 252 observations; inputs are lagged by two business days. However, the 13 joint scenarios are model-output paths, not draws from a fitted joint return distribution. No correlated residual simulation, copula, multivariate bootstrap or covariance-matching step is applied. Choosing the same method for all assets does not by itself preserve their forecast correlation. These VSS/EVPI values therefore describe uncertainty across forecasting methods, not all market uncertainty.

Definitions follow the maximisation convention in mpi-sppy documentation and the Notre Dame stochastic-optimisation example. At exact optimality WS ≥ RP ≥ EEV; this ordering alone does not certify a heuristic result.

1.4.g. All first-stage solutions, objectives and information timing

This subsection exposes saved first-stage vectors: the frozen no-sale baseline, EV, EEV, the diagnostic RP re-solve and 13 WS solutions. EV and EEV deliberately have identical first-stage units. Main is the current corrected trade plan when present. Active is the frozen no-sale baseline; Sale is the archived unrestricted-sales diagnostic, not an executable recommendation. RP is a diagnostic alternative; WS assumes perfect foresight and is not a set of scenario-contingent orders to place today. Main and BothSignal use the corrected signal gates and observed-prefix nodes; all EV/EEV/RP/WS rows retain the original no-sale constraints. No allocation is changed here.

1.4.g.d. Information timing: what is known now and what recourse means

At the first decision: historical observations, current holdings, latest known prices/NAVs, liquidity inputs, model forecasts and scenario probabilities are available. The realised future scenario is unknown. One common q₀ is chosen for all scenarios. The forecasts already influence that choice through the expected complete-policy objective; q₀ is not optimised on historical data alone.

At recourse: the model allows additional purchases after 3 November, τ = 2 in the five-date forecast grid. The simulated Current-portfolio change since the origin defines a down/flat/up node using ±0.1%. Every scenario in the same node shares the same second-stage quantity vector. For the current inputs only flat and up nodes occur. Forecast prices are used to simulate trading and wealth; no actual future observations have been downloaded or used. The contingent decisions are planned today and would be executed only after the corresponding information is observed. q₀ and all node-contingent second-stage quantities are optimised jointly today; this is not a procedure that waits for actual future data and then reruns the optimiser. This calculation is not a live receding-horizon trading system.

NodeSignalScenario countScenario labels
1Flat7AR(1)-GARCH-t; Damped ETS; Dependency Extra Trees; Dependency Gradient boosting; Extra Trees; Gradient boosting; No change
2Up6ARIMA(1,1,1); Dependency Ridge; Historical drift; Neural network MLP; Ridge regression; Validation ensemble
$$ c_0=B-p_0^{\mathsf T}q_0,\qquad q_{n(s)}\ge q_0\ge q^{\mathrm{current}},\qquad c_s=c_0+p_{\tau,s}^{\mathsf T}(q_0-q_{n(s)}). $$
$$ V_{t,s}=\begin{cases} p_{t,s}^{\mathsf T}q_0+c_0,&t\le\tau,\\ p_{t,s}^{\mathsf T}q_{n(s)}+c_s,&t>\tau, \end{cases}\qquad r^{\mathrm{future}}_{t,s}=\frac{V_{t,s}}{V_{t-1,s}}-1. $$

Here B = EUR 15,000; p₀ is the vector of latest known prices; pₜ,ₛ is the forecast price vector at date t in scenario s; q₀ is the common first-stage holding; qₙ₍ₛ₎ is the post-recourse holding for the observed node; c₀ and cₛ are cash before and after recourse. Purchases are self-financing and existing units cannot be sold.

Important qualification — the implemented historical block: the optimisation does not append forecast returns to a history fixed at q₀ weights. It backcasts the post-recourse portfolio through historical asset returns, with weights marked at scenario-specific recourse prices:

$$ w_{i,s}^{\mathrm{backcast}}= \frac{p_{\tau,s,i}\,q_{n(s),i}}{p_{\tau,s}^{\mathsf T}q_{n(s)}+c_s},\qquad r_{h,s}^{\mathrm{backcast}}=\sum_i H_{h,i}\,w_{i,s}^{\mathrm{backcast}}. $$
$$ z=\sum_{s=1}^{13}\frac1{13}\left[ \operatorname{netSD}\!\left( (r_{1,s}^{\mathrm{backcast}},\ldots,r_{272,s}^{\mathrm{backcast}}, r_{1,s}^{\mathrm{future}},\ldots,r_{5,s}^{\mathrm{future}});\,\mathcal R_s \right)-P(q_{n(s)},p_{\tau,s})\right]. $$

Hₕ,ᵢ is observed historical asset i return at date h; ℛₛ is the frozen comparison universe with that scenario's forecast extension; P is the existing portfolio penalty. Cash has zero return. This is the objective actually implemented and used for the reported VSS/EVPI estimates. Future decisions do not change observed H, but they change the portfolio weights used to evaluate it. Thus the historical portfolio block is a hypothetical scenario-dependent backcast, not the realised return history of holdings bought today.

Consequences: first-stage and recourse decisions obey the information-node restrictions, but it would be inaccurate to describe the full criterion as an immutable first-stage historical portfolio plus only forward-looking recourse returns. The historical-only table above uses a separate fixed q₀ diagnostic, with weights p₀,ᵢq₀,ᵢ/B, to make this distinction visible. No forecasting or optimisation rule has been silently changed in this audit. If the intended criterion keeps historical portfolio weights fixed at the first-stage decision, the backcast term must instead use p₀,ᵢq₀,ᵢ/B in every scenario. That would be a model change requiring new optimisation and new VSS/EVPI calculations; it has not been applied here.

Sale is an archived unrestricted-sales diagnostic. Main and BothSignal, when present, use the new signal constraints and observed-prefix nodes. WS01–WS13 and VSS/EVPI remain the original no-sale experiments.

1.4.h. Comparison: signal-gated sales allowed at both stages

Comparison: sales may also occur initially, but only when the current indicators give at least three SELL votes and the equally weighted terminal forecast is below the latest price. Recourse uses the same scenario-specific gate as the main policy. No shorting, borrowing or unconditional sale is allowed.

Expected netSD 0.902857; objective 0.883806; initial sales 0.

Why this solution equals the main one: no currently held asset meets the initial sale condition. The two admissible sets coincide for this snapshot, so the same optimised policy is reused; this is not evidence that allowing sales can never help.

1.4.i. Comparison: no sales at either stage

Comparison only: the frozen original policy prohibits sales at both stages and uses its original down/flat/up information nodes. It is no longer the main trade plan.

Full-catalogue quantity search: all 86 history/forecast-eligible instruments (63 shares and 23 funds) are modelled; purchases remain subject to liquidity and minimum-lot rules. The decision quantities are searched directly, not chosen from five legacy portfolios. Seven threads evaluate integer moves. This nonconvex heuristic has no global-optimality certificate; the coverage table records proposals and feasible proposals for each variable.

Expected scenario netSD 0.862857; expected penalty 0.032627; objective 0.830230. Historical first-stage netSD 0.862857 is a separate diagnostic. Every scenario contains 272 common historical returns (2025-10-01–2026-10-29) plus all five forecast dates, 2–6 November. The enlarged frozen reference system has denominator 175; older numerical scores from the smaller universe must not be substituted.

First-stage decisions are common to all scenarios. After 3 November, scenarios with the same observed Current-return node (below −0.1%, within ±0.1%, above +0.1%) share recourse quantities. No existing positions can be sold. The 15,000 EUR budget includes cash; later trades are self-financing. Two to four funds, whole units, minimum fund value EUR 300 and at least 10 units in new stock positions apply. The share liquidity rule is unchanged: typical weekly volume at least five times the total holding, at least 80% active sessions out of 65, and at least four out of the last five. MOLNR cannot be purchased.

Shares with nonpositive individual historical netSD cannot be increased; existing units are retained. RKB1R remains reference-only by the earlier explicit exclusion. Every offered fund with enough history is considered; there is no fixed three-fund basket or mandatory emerging-market allocation.

Target invested EUR 14,165.38; cash EUR 834.62; OUT / IN 151 / 0; netSD 0.862857. Average annual historical cash dividends EUR 429.26; embedded annual fund costs approximately EUR 9.00. Accumulating funds make no cash dividend payment.

All eligible coordinates are proposed in the first stage and every observed recourse node. A proposal can fail the budget, fund count, minimum lot, liquidity or mean floor. No global optimum is claimed. Funds without enough observations and shares without usable histories are listed in the catalogue rather than silently discarded. Unavailable individual methods use an explicitly registered No change scenario path; this is not a claim that the failed method fitted.
Mathematical model $$\max_{q,c_0,\{y_s,c_s\}}\frac1{13}\sum_s\left[\frac{OUT_s(q,y_s)-IN_s(q,y_s)}{175}-P_s(y_s)\right].$$ $$\sum_i p_{i0}q_i+c_0=15000,\quad c_s=c_0+\sum_i p_{is\tau}(q_i-y_{is})\ge0.$$ $$q_i\ge q_i^{Current},\quad y_{is}\ge q_i,\quad q_i,y_{is}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\quad g(s)=g(s')\Rightarrow y_{is}=y_{is'}.$$ $$\mathcal X_s=\{R^{hist}_{1s},\ldots,R^{hist}_{272,s},R_{s1},\ldots,R_{s5}\}.$$

Asset index i runs across the complete forecast-eligible catalogue, not a preselected fund trio. Historical portfolio weights freeze the final allocation including cash; forecast returns follow the two-stage wealth path. Exact empirical dominance checks include TSD interior extrema and its mean condition. The original position-count, effective-count, small-stock-position and dividend penalties remain, plus the 0.002 squared liquidity-utilisation penalty. Recurring fund expenses already enter NAV returns. Execution delays, bid–ask spreads and taxes remain unmodelled.

2. Market analysis — Baltic and global HMM regimes

External market regimes: five Baltic indices define local conditions and MSCI World defines global conditions. 4,820 common observations, 2007-01-04–2026-11-05. At the last common date the estimated regime is R3: global stress only. This is a statistical volatility state, not a guarantee that prices will rise.

Market analysis is section 2; portfolio analysis follows in section 3. All market-model estimation uses R: depmixS4 and markovchain. The resulting external regimes are ready for a subsequent market-conditioned scenario design; existing allocation quantities are not reoptimised in this market-identification step.

Matrix stability check: first-order bootstrap p = 0.134; time-homogeneity bootstrap p = 0.002. The full-history matrix varies over time in the data and is presented as a historical summary. Recent-window comparisons and the implications for forecasting are in 2.7.

2.1. Data, index identities and observation calendar

Exact indices are used, not ETF proxies. MSCI World is the official index code 990100, EUR, gross total return (GRTR). OMXB10 is the requested price index; the other local indices are gross-return indices. This variant difference is disclosed rather than silently replacing OMX Baltic 10 with OMXB10GI.

Identical duplicate Nasdaq endpoint rows and its non-observation previous-close chart anchor are removed. Conflicting duplicate closes cause a validation failure. No missing close is forward-filled. Log returns are calculated after taking the intersection of observed closing dates, so all indices cover the same intervals. One initial return is then removed for lagged regressors. A step is one common observation interval, which can span more than one calendar or exchange trading day.

Some individual series reach 2026-11-02, but Vilnius closes make 2026-10-30 the latest complete joint observation. The headline regime is dated accordingly. Local and global closes occur at different times; lagged market regressors avoid using the later same-day global close as a Baltic predictor.

2.2. Two-state HMM specification and estimation

Two Gaussian HMMs with two hidden states are fitted for each index. The first uses that index's returns; the second additionally uses the previous common-observation returns of the other five indices. Means/regression coefficients and residual SD depend on the hidden state; transition probabilities are constant within each fitted model.

$$x_{it}=100\log\frac{I_{it}}{I_{i,t-1}},\quad S_{it}^{(m)}\in\{0,1\},\quad \Pr(S_{it}^{(m)}=b\mid S_{i,t-1}^{(m)}=a)=A_{iab}^{(m)}.$$
$$m=1:\quad x_{it}\mid S_{it}^{(1)}=s\sim\mathcal N(\mu_{is},\sigma_{is}^{2}),\\m=2:\quad x_{it}\mid S_{it}^{(2)}=s,\mathbf x_{-i,t-1}\sim\mathcal N\left(\beta_{is0}+\sum_{j\ne i}\beta_{isj}x_{j,t-1},\sigma_{is}^{2}\right).$$

I is the index close; x is the log return in percent; i and j identify indices; t identifies a common observation; m is the method; s is the latent state; A is a two-state transition matrix; μ is the state mean; β are state-specific regression coefficients; σ is residual SD. The state with larger σ is labelled stress. Stress can include large positive returns and does not mean every observation is a loss.

Six seeded initialisations are tried for each two-state full-history and training-only fit. Selection uses the highest finite likelihood among valid converged starts, not a desired regime frequency. Degenerate SD or a state with fewer than 20 posterior-weighted observations is rejected. The competing one-state model is fitted to the identical response and predictors. All twelve selected full-history fits converged.

$$q_{it}^{(m)}=\Pr(S_{it}^{(m)}=1\mid x_{1:T}),\quad d_{it}^{(m)}=\mathbf1\{q_{it}^{(m)}>0.5\},\quad L_{it}=1+\frac{d_{it}^{(1)}+d_{it}^{(2)}}2.$$

These retrospective q values come from depmixS4::forwardbackward() smoothing. Thresholding posterior probabilities is not Viterbi path decoding. Filtered probabilities condition only on observations up to t; full-fit filtering still uses parameters estimated on the complete sample. Genuine held-out filtering below instead freezes all parameters at the training boundary.

2.3. Baltic local-market state
$$L_t^B=\frac15\sum_{i\in\mathcal B}L_{it},\qquad b_t=\mathbf1\{L_t^B\ge1.3\}.$$

𝓑 contains the five requested Baltic indices. Each index receives weight 1/5 and each HMM method weight 1/2: at least three of the ten method–index stress votes trigger the local stress state. This is a weighted voting level, not a calibrated probability. Because the regional indices overlap in constituents, ten votes are not ten independent observations.

Figure 2.b. Baltic-index stress probabilities: own history and lagged market information
Figure 2.c. Aggregated local and global stress levels with the equity threshold
2.4. Global MSCI World state
$$L_t^G=L_{\mathrm{MSCI},t},\qquad g_t=\mathbf1\{L_t^G\ge1.3\}.$$

The global signal uses MSCI World with the same two-method aggregation. Since its possible levels are 1, 1.5 and 2, either method voting stress is sufficient at threshold 1.3. Both regions are equity markets: the bond-specific threshold 1.5 from the systemic-risk paper is not mechanically relabelled as a global-equity rule. Threshold sensitivity is reported below.

Figure 2.d. MSCI World returns, inferred global stress and model probabilities
2.5. Four combined market regimes
$$R_t=1+b_t+2g_t\in\{1,2,3,4\}.$$

The four states combine a local Baltic condition with a global MSCI World condition. This changes the economic interpretation of the original stock/bond split; it is not a claim that global equities behave like bonds.

2.6. Markov transition matrix and regime characteristics
$$\pi=\pi\widehat P,\quad\sum_i\pi_i=1,\quad\mathbb E[D_i]=\frac1{1-\widehat P_{ii}},\quad\mathbb E[T_i^+]=\frac1{\pi_i},\\m_{jj}=0,\quad m_{ij}=1+\sum_{k\ne j}\widehat P_{ik}m_{kj}\quad(i\ne j).$$
$$N_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\mathbf1\{R_t=i,R_{t+1}=j\},\qquad\widehat P_{ij}=\frac{N_{ij}}{\sum_kN_{ik}},\quad\sum_j\widehat P_{ij}=1.$$

Rows are the current regime and columns the next regime. All four states are represented; no transition row is fabricated. This joint matrix is estimated from the combined observed regime sequence, not from a Kronecker product assuming independent Baltic/global chains.

Examples: R1 persistence is 96.23% per common observation; its model-implied mean spell is 26.52 steps. The fixed-matrix mean first passage R1→R4 is 120.47 steps; R4→R1 is 27.66. These are historical homogeneous-chain characteristics, not dates when a crisis or recovery must occur. Recurrence 1/π includes a return at the very next step when the state does not change; it is not the waiting time after leaving that state. The first-passage diagonal is zero, while recurrence is a separate quantity.

Higher persistence is useful when the regime is calm, but means longer stress when the regime is stressed. A higher model-implied R4 share means more frequent joint stress; a longer R1→R4 first-passage time means a longer model-implied wait for joint stress; a shorter R4→R1 time means faster return to calm. All such comparisons remain conditional on the fixed-matrix approximation.

2.7. Diagnostics, time variation and held-out validation

First-order Markov check: conditional-on-label bootstrap p = 0.134. The first-order approximation is not rejected, which is not proof that aggregation of hidden chains is itself Markov.

Time homogeneity is rejected: bootstrap p = 0.002. Transition patterns changed across the historical sample. The full-period matrix, stationary probabilities, first-passage times and fixed-P horizon curves are descriptive model characteristics, not validated invariant future probabilities. Recent-window estimates and historical blocks are provided to expose that change.

2.9. Transition-matrix stress sensitivity

The stress-test adaptation multiplies worsening transitions 1→2, 1→3, 1→4, 2→4 and 3→4 by k, leaves other off-diagonal transitions unchanged, and adjusts each diagonal to preserve its row sum. Regimes 2 and 3 are not intrinsically ordered as better/worse than one another.

$$P^{(k)}_{ij}=k\widehat P_{ij}\quad((i,j)\in\{(1,2),(1,3),(1,4),(2,4),(3,4)\}),\qquad P^{(k)}_{ii}=1-\sum_{j\ne i}P^{(k)}_{ij}.$$

This experiment perturbs a historical matrix; it is not an estimated probability of an actual future crisis and does not generate new portfolio trades.

2.10. Methodology sources and adaptation

The first paper motivates separate binary hidden states, a four-regime combination, transition estimates, stationary and first-passage characteristics, and worsening-transition stress tests. The second adds per-index own-history/market-conditioned estimation and weighted aggregation. Here stocks/bonds are replaced by Baltic/global equities, predictors are lagged, both equity thresholds are 1.3, and probabilities are explicitly posterior-threshold decoded. This implementation uses EM-fitted Gaussian HMMs in depmixS4; it does not implement the separate Lavielle–Lebarbier MCMC change-point procedure discussed in the first paper.

Stress testing for IInd pillar life-cycle pension funds using hidden Markov model; Systemic risk assessment through connectedness and spillover; depmixS4 methods; markovchain methods.

Figure 3.e. SSD pairwise dominance matrix used by netSD A blue cell equals 1 when the row entity SSD-dominates the column entity. Row sums contribute to OUT; column sums contribute to IN.
Figure 3.f. TSD pairwise dominance matrix used by netSD A blue cell equals 1 when the row entity TSD-dominates the column entity, including the required mean-return condition.
Figure 3.g. Combined FSD + SSD + TSD matrix used to calculate netSD Each cell is the sum of the three order-specific indicators and therefore ranges from 0 to 3. For every entity, OUT is its combined row sum and IN is its combined column sum. The frozen full-universe denominator is 175; netSD = (OUT − IN) / 175. The same reference matrix is used for all historical diagnostics; scenario outcomes additionally append the scenario week.

Every forecast-eligible share is scored, including illiquid names that cannot be purchased. Missing-history instruments are documented in section 1.4.d.

The five-year average yield uses ex-dividend amounts divided by the latest available price on or before each ex-date. Current- and update-quantity dividend amounts use the five-year average annual dividend per share; they are historical gross scenarios, not forecasts. allocation_change_direction describes the optimiser's target relative to current holdings. It is not the current execution recommendation; use current_execution_decision in the canonical trade table and interactive share profiles for that purpose.

VAR, VECM, GARCH and DCC connectedness The connectedness analysis follows the VAR/VECM and generalized forecast-error variance-decomposition logic used by [Kabašinskas (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13362-024-00144-x). The main network contains every investment-admissible share, all 12 funds and the S&P 500; the portfolio network is retained as a secondary comparison. The arrowhead identifies the direction: A → B means that shocks in A explain part of B's forecast-error variance. An asterisk (*) after a value means that this direction is significant in the corresponding Granger-causality test at 5%. **Red nodes are net receivers (TO − FROM < 0); blue nodes are net transmitters (TO − FROM > 0).** Node area increases with |TO − FROM|, so a larger node has a stronger net role. **Model-assumption checks are shown before the results.** ADF tests should reject a unit root for VAR returns. VECM requires non-stationary levels, stationary first differences and a cointegration rank strictly between zero and the number of variables. Stability is required for VAR. The residual-whiteness p-value should exceed 0.05. Multivariate normality fails in every case, which is common for financial returns but makes Gaussian small-sample inference less reliable. The high-dimensional Johansen critical values are outside the tabulated range of the software, so the share VECM rank is exploratory. A failed row is displayed for comparison and must not be treated as a validated structural model.

GARCH volatility spillover and DCC-GARCH The GARCH analysis uses a retrospective non-trading correction before model estimation. Consecutive zero returns are treated as stale-price days: the next observed non-zero log return is spread equally over that zero-return spell and its trade day. Corrected returns are then winsorised at the 0.5% and 99.5% quantiles. Shares with more than 40% zero-return observations are excluded from this subsection. This correction reduces stale-price distortion but is an explicit modelling assumption and must not be interpreted as observed daily price movement. The filter excludes **RSU1L, TEL1L, TVE1T** from the GARCH/DCC system only. They remain in the other portfolio analyses. After filtering, 31 series and 857 common observations remain. #### Liquidity-corrected GARCH variance spillover Each retained series is fitted with a Student-t GARCH(1,1). A VAR is then fitted to the log conditional variances, and its 10-step generalized FEVD produces directional volatility spillovers. The enlarged arrowhead shows the direction of predictive transmission between conditional variances. An asterisk marks variance Granger causality at 5%; red nodes are net volatility receivers, blue nodes are net transmitters, and node area increases with |TO − FROM|. The corrected-volatility Total Spillover Index is **41.57%**. **18 of 31** univariate fits still have α + β ≥ 0.99, so volatility persistence remains close to the IGARCH boundary and the long-horizon interpretation requires caution.

DCC-GARCH conditional correlations (not spillover) Following [Engle (2002)](https://doi.org/10.1198/073500102288618487), standardized residuals from the univariate GARCH models enter the two-step Dynamic Conditional Correlation recursion. DCC is an undirected conditional-dependence model and must not be read as Granger causality or directional shock transmission. The left panel is a hierarchically clustered heatmap of average conditional correlations. The upper-right panel shows their mean absolute strength through time; the lower-right panel shows the five pairs with the strongest average DCC. The parameters are estimated from six starting values to guard against a local boundary solution. The estimated DCC parameters are α = **0.0107**, β = **0.7664**, and α + β = **0.7771**; optimiser convergence = **True**. The very small DCC persistence means that, after the stale-price correction, the estimated conditional-correlation system is close to a constant-correlation model with brief isolated spikes rather than a slowly evolving dependence process.

Median daily turnover and zero-volume frequency use official Nasdaq Baltic price-volume observations from the last 365 calendar days of the sample. Trade-to-turnover is the proposed absolute order value divided by median daily turnover. HIGH flags median turnover below EUR 5,000 or an order above 20% of median turnover; MEDIUM flags below EUR 20,000 or above 10%. These are transparent screening thresholds, not a guarantee of execution. HIGH trades should be split, limited or omitted after checking the live order book.

The number of holdings is not a diversification measure. Top-five and top-ten shares show how much capital is concentrated in the largest positions; HHI and the effective number of positions measure weight concentration. Country, list, industry and supersector totals expose common economic exposures that a position count conceals. Very small positions add trading complexity while making little difference to risk. ### In-sample, out-of-sample and complete-period validation netSD counts outgoing minus incoming FSD, SSD and TSD relations relative to a fixed comparison network. It has no monetary unit and does not state expected profit, maximum loss or suitability for an investor. Use it as a distribution-ranking signal together with return, volatility, drawdown, VaR/ES, liquidity, concentration and cost results. The S&P 500 series is a USD price-index benchmark. It excludes dividends and has not been converted into EUR investor returns, so it is retained only as a broad market sensitivity reference. Direct performance claims require a total-return benchmark converted to EUR over identical dates. Share returns are close-to-close price returns, excluding cash dividends; accumulating-fund NAV returns include reinvested income and recurring expenses. This is not a strictly like-for-like total-return comparison. The dividend-shortfall penalty uses historical five-year cash distributions, not forecast payouts. Historical dividends do not establish future sustainability; earnings quality, debt and payout coverage require a separate fundamental review.
3.14. Model

Active full-universe, two-stage no-sales model

Mathematical model $$\max_{q,c_0,\{y_s,c_s\}}\frac1{13}\sum_s\left[\frac{OUT_s(q,y_s)-IN_s(q,y_s)}{175}-P_s(y_s)\right].$$ $$\sum_i p_{i0}q_i+c_0=15000,\quad c_s=c_0+\sum_i p_{is\tau}(q_i-y_{is})\ge0.$$ $$q_i\ge q_i^{Current},\quad y_{is}\ge q_i,\quad q_i,y_{is}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\quad g(s)=g(s')\Rightarrow y_{is}=y_{is'}.$$ $$\mathcal X_s=\{R^{hist}_{1s},\ldots,R^{hist}_{272,s},R_{s1},\ldots,R_{s5}\}.$$

Asset index i runs across the complete forecast-eligible catalogue, not a preselected fund trio. Historical portfolio weights freeze the final allocation including cash; forecast returns follow the two-stage wealth path. Exact empirical dominance checks include TSD interior extrema and its mean condition. The original position-count, effective-count, small-stock-position and dividend penalties remain, plus the 0.002 squared liquidity-utilisation penalty. Recurring fund expenses already enter NAV returns. Execution delays, bid–ask spreads and taxes remain unmodelled.

Archived restricted benchmark formulations — not the active execution model

Selected Update3 no-sales basket: Emerging Europe, World and Japan

The following restricted search determines the selected no-sales plan. The sales-allowed model above is retained separately. Define $C(\mathbf u)=\sum_f v_fu_fc_f$ (EUR/year), $C_{\max}=15.05802624$, and let $P(\mathbf w)$ denote the sum of the original four penalties. $$\max_{\mathbf q,\mathbf u}\quad\operatorname{netSD}(\mathbf w)-0.001\frac{C(\mathbf u)}{C_{\max}}-0.0001P(\mathbf w).$$ $$\mathcal F=\{\text{Emerging Europe C},\ \text{Access Edge Global C},\ \text{Access Edge Japan C}\},\quad u_f=0\quad(f\notin\mathcal F).$$ $$v_fu_f\ge300\quad(f\in\mathcal F),\qquad C(\mathbf u)\le C_{\max},\qquad q_i\ge q_i^{\mathrm{Current}}.$$ The EUR 15,000 budget, integer quantities, positive-netSD purchase eligibility, minimum 10 units for new stock positions and minimum mean-return constraints above also apply. The legacy restricted model used denominator 133; the current full-universe model in section 1.4 uses frozen denominator 175. The cost and penalty terms are small tie-breakers relative to a $1/133$ netSD step. NAV returns already include ongoing fund expenses; no second cost deduction is made. The selected whole-unit quantities are a numerical result, not a global optimality certificate.

Update3: shares and funds in the penalised netSD model

Let $q_i$ be integer stock quantities, $u_f$ integer fund units, $p_i$ share prices and $v_f$ published EUR NAV. Portfolio weights are their invested EUR values divided by total invested capital. Fund NAV returns already include recurring expenses. $$\max_{\mathbf q,\mathbf u}\quad \operatorname{netSD}(\mathbf w)-\lambda_N N_{\mathrm{new,shares}}^2-\lambda_E\frac{1}{\sum_jw_j^2}-\lambda_S P_{\mathrm{small,new,shares}}-\lambda_D P_{\mathrm{dividend,shares}}$$ $$\sum_i p_iq_i+\sum_fv_fu_f\le15000,\qquad q_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\quad u_f\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0},\quad\sum_jw_j=1.$$ $$2\le\sum_fz_f\le4,\quad z_f\in\{0,1\},\quad0.02z_f\le w_f\le z_f.$$ $$q_i\ge q_i^{\mathrm{Current}}\quad\text{in the no-sales case};\qquad \boldsymbol\mu^\top\mathbf w\ge\mu_{\mathrm{Current}}.$$ New stock purchases are either zero or at least 10 shares. Funds use whole units and are exempt from the cash-dividend shortfall penalty because the selected C classes accumulate income. Estimated embedded annual expense is $\sum_f(v_fu_f)c_f$; it is disclosed in EUR and is not subtracted from net NAV returns a second time. No fund is compulsory. The Russia exclusion, when Emerging Europe is selected, follows its mandate; the absence of China is monitored from published holdings and is not a permanent contractual exclusion. ### Exact mathematical formulation of the netSD portfolio For share $j$ and observation $t$, let $R_{tj}$ be the return, $w_j$ the portfolio weight and $$r_{p,t}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_jR_{tj},\qquad \sum_{j=1}^{n}w_j=1,\qquad w_j\ge0.$$ For entity $i$, define the empirical distribution and its successive integrals by $$H_i^{(1)}(x)=F_i(x),\qquad H_i^{(q)}(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}H_i^{(q-1)}(u)\,du,\quad q=2,3.$$ Entity $i$ dominates entity $k$ at order $q$ when $$H_i^{(q)}(x)\le H_k^{(q)}(x)\quad\text{for every observed support point }x,$$ with strict inequality for at least one point. Third-order dominance additionally requires $\mathbb E(R_i)\ge\mathbb E(R_k)$. Write $a_{ik}^{(q)}=1$ when these conditions hold and zero otherwise. Then $$\operatorname{OUT}(p)=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\sum_{q=1}^{3}a_{pk}^{(q)},\qquad \operatorname{IN}(p)=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\sum_{q=1}^{3}a_{kp}^{(q)},$$ $$\boxed{\operatorname{netSD}(p)=\frac{\operatorname{OUT}(p)-\operatorname{IN}(p)}{D}},\qquad D=\max_i\{\operatorname{OUT}(i)+\operatorname{IN}(i)\}.$$ The unpenalised portfolio problem is $$\boxed{\max_{\mathbf w}\;\operatorname{netSD}(\mathbf w)}$$ subject to $$\sum_jw_j=1,\qquad w_j\ge0,\qquad \boldsymbol\mu^\top\mathbf w\ge\mu_{\mathrm{Current}},$$ $$w_j=0\quad\text{if individual }\operatorname{netSD}_j\le0\text{ or the share is outside the admissible universe}.$$ The common-network scores in Section 3.1 supersede numerical score quotes from the previous share-only reference universe. NetSD is discrete and the numerical search does not certify a global optimum.
3.15. Data coverage

The official catalogue contains 91 instruments: 67 Nasdaq Baltic shares and 24 Swedbank-managed mutual funds offered by Swedbank Lithuania. Forecasts cover 86 instruments. Share closes are through 30 October 2026; the newest available EUR fund NAVs are dated 29 October. Comparable portfolio diagnostics use 272 returns from 2025-10-01 through 2026-10-29, because younger funds lack earlier histories. Longer individual histories still enter their forecast fits.
